newsitem.title: UK: Aid official accuses Kabila troops of massacres.
newsitem.headline: Aid official accuses Kabila troops of massacres.

text.p: A leading aid official on Monday said forces loyal to Laurent Kabila had killed many thousands of Hutu refugees in former Zaire and said he was convinced massacres were still continuing.
"There has been systematic widespread killing of refugees for several months," the official, who asked not to be identified, told reporters.
"It's probably the largest loss of refugee life in recent times...the speculation is tens of thousands. No one knows how many tens of thousands," he said, adding:
"I've not had a report in the last three days but I think the killings are continuing."

Kabila took power in the last month over what is Africa's third largest country -- renamed the Democratic Republic of Congo -- amid widespread reports his forces have been systematically killing Hutu refugees.
Over a million Hutus fled Rwanda in 1994, fearing reprisals after Hutu hardliners slaughtered hundreds of thousands of minority Tutsis.
The alleged victims of Kabila's forces and his Rwandan Tutsi allies had fled further west into Congo when the majority returned to Rwanda. Many are still missing in the dense rainforests.
"We can't account for 200,000 to 250,000 Rwandan refugees and 20,000 to 30,000 Burundi refugees," the official said.

A top U.S. aid official said last week Washington believed massacres were continuing in the east of former Zaire and reported what he said was a systematic effort to cover up atrocities in the region.
Kabila has promised an investigation into the allegations but the aid official said on Monday there were signs that evidence was already being destroyed.
"Once the investigators get into the rain forests and try to go the dirt tracks to reach the alleged mass graves -- that's the real test," he said.

The official also said the repatriation of Hutus from the killing grounds to Rwanda was fraught with disaster since the returnees -- now based in refugee camps ine western Rwanda -- were fighting Tutsis once again.
"The Hutu-Tutsi conflict is far from over...there are ongoing clashes in all areas," he said. "In Rwanda, (aid workers say) the polarisation is the greatest it has been in recent times."
The Rwandan government had exacerbated the situation by refusing to give returnees their land back and denying them western food aid, he said.
"We know people are dying from starvation because the government is not sending them food."
The official said the only way to restore peace to the Great Lakes region was to send in a western miltary force but he harboured few hopes.
"Aid agencies can't protect refugees unless they have political backing and frankly that political backing has been lacking in the Great Lakes region since 1994."
A senior U.N. refugee agency official said on Saturday that it planned to separate former soldiers and militiamen from over 100,000 Rwandan Hutu refugees scattered throughout Central Africa.

Assistant High Commissioner for Refugees, Sergio Viera de Mello, said those suspected of genocide in Rwanda would be handed over for trial but that this could only happen with the participation of those involved.
